section.title: Motion revisited
section.p: The derivative began as velocity. Then it became slope, local linear approximation, and a function of position along a graph. Now the original motion story returns, but with sharper language.
A position function tells where an object is. Its derivative tells how fast that position is changing. The derivative of the derivative tells how fast the velocity is changing.

paragraphs.title: Units
paragraphs.p: If position is measured in meters and time in seconds, then
s(t) has units of meters,
v(t)=s'(t) has units of meters/second,
and
a(t)=v'(t) has units of meters/second^2.
The units explain the meaning. Acceleration measures how many meters per second of velocity are gained or lost each second.

subsection.title: Speed versus velocity
subsection.p: Velocity has a sign. Speed does not.
If the positive direction is to the right, then v(t)\gt 0 means the object is moving right, while v(t)\lt 0 means the object is moving left.

subsection.title: Falling under constant acceleration
subsection.p: Near the surface of the earth, if air resistance is ignored, falling objects have nearly constant acceleration.
If we measure height upward, then gravity pulls in the negative direction. In feet, the acceleration is approximately -32\text{ ft/s}^2. In meters, it is approximately -9.8\text{ m/s}^2.
The sign is not a property of gravity alone. It also depends on our choice of positive direction. If upward is positive, gravity is negative. If downward is positive, gravity is positive.

subsection.title: Units and signs in motion problems
subsection.p: The hardest part of many motion problems is not differentiating. It is deciding what the signs mean.
A position is measured relative to an origin. A velocity is measured relative to a positive direction. Acceleration tells whether velocity is increasing or decreasing in that chosen direction.

subsection.p: Acceleration does not directly tell which way the object is moving. Velocity does that. Acceleration tells how velocity is changing.

paragraphs.title: Speeding up and slowing down
paragraphs.p: Because speed is |v(t)|, an object speeds up when the magnitude of velocity increases.
For motion along a line:
paragraphs.md: \text{if \(v\) and \(a\) have the same sign, the object is speeding up,}
paragraphs.p: and
paragraphs.md: \text{if \(v\) and \(a\) have opposite signs, the object is slowing down.}
paragraphs.p: For the ball y(t)=64t-16t^2, we have v(t)=64-32t, a(t)=-32.
For 0\lt t\lt 2, v(t)\gt 0 and a(t)\lt 0. The signs are opposite, so the ball is slowing down as it rises.
For 2\lt t\lt 4, v(t)\lt 0 and a(t)\lt 0. The signs are the same, so the ball is speeding up as it falls.

paragraphs.title: Same physical motion, different sign convention
paragraphs.p: Suppose a stone is dropped from a 100-meter tower.
If height above the ground is the position, and upward is positive, then
The velocity is v(t)=-9.8t, and the acceleration is a(t)=-9.8. Both velocity and acceleration are negative after the stone is released, so the stone is speeding up downward.
If instead we measure downward distance from the release point, then the same motion is described by
Then r'(t)=9.8t, and r''(t)=9.8. Now velocity and acceleration are positive because the positive direction has been chosen downward.
The physics did not change. The coordinate choice changed.

statement.p: Before interpreting signs, choose: origin and positive direction. Only then do signs have meaning.

subsection.p: The derivative has now returned to its first meaning: instantaneous motion. But even motion can hide traps. A graph may look continuous and still have no velocity at a sharp turn. A derivative may exist and still behave unexpectedly. Before moving to a larger library of differentiation rules, we pause to collect these warning examples.
